topics_down_more.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry. The model is constructed by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, specifically utilizing the same rotation symmetry that protects the topological crystalline insulator phase. The model exhibits distinctive topological responses characteristic of rotation-protected topological crystalline insulators, including topological responses that emerge from the rotation symmetry protecting this topological crystalline insulator and topological responses that reflect the underlying structure of this rotation-protected topological crystalline insulator. These topological responses are mathematically described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field that corresponds to the underlying rotation symmetry of the topological crystalline insulator. The filled bands of this topological crystalline insulator model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, presenting a fundamental obstruction in the characterization of the topological crystalline insulator phase. However, this Wannier obstruction can be removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals to the model, which reveals that the topology is of the fragile type rather than being stable. The fragile nature of the topology in this topological crystalline insulator implies that the response properties can be derived by representing the model as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients, where these atomic orbitals restore the Wannier representation that was obstructed in the original topological crystalline insulator. This prototypical two-dimensional topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry serves to illustrate general principles applicable to all topological crystalline insulators protected by point group symmetries. We demonstrate that dimensional reduction techniques can map the problem of classifying two-dimensional topological crystalline insulators protected by rotation to a lower-dimensional problem, and this mapping enables us to obtain the complete classification of such rotation-protected topological crystalline insulators as well as the modification of this classification.
topics_down_more.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence approach for chess problem composition called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). It uses selected attributes from chess positions and recombines them in such a way as to generate new chess attributes that can then be used to create novel chess problems of creative value to chess enthusiasts and composers. This allows some of the burden of chess problem composition to be passed from human chess composers to automated chess composition systems. The approach was tested extensively in chess problem composition. We used it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from existing chess problems and existing chess problems already created by others. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing computational chess aesthetics model designed specifically for evaluating chess problem quality. The computer-generated chess problems were also assessed using the same chess problem evaluation approach that had been applied to the automatically generated chess problems mentioned earlier. The results suggest that chess attributes collected and recombined from different chess sources using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality according to established chess aesthetic principles. In particular, one chess source consisting of certain chess problem sequences was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to those generated using another chess source consisting of different chess compositions, and the first chess source proved more efficient as well in generating acceptable chess problems. Why certain chess information sources prove more productive than others for automated chess problem generation remains an open question requiring further chess composition research using the DSNS approach for chess problem composition. The DSNS approach is, in principle, scalable to generating additional chess problems through continued application of the chess attribute extraction and recombination methodology.
topics_down_more.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex dynamical systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest in dynamical systems is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the dynamics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints for these systems. Not surprisingly, approximating complex dynamical systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations of system behavior has become common practice, as illustrated by the numerous successful examples of learned dynamical system models. However, generalizability of the dynamical system models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the system dynamics. We tackle these issues in dynamical system learning from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy for training system models. In curriculum learning for dynamical systems, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple dynamical samples towards more complex system trajectories in order to favor convergence and generalization of the learned dynamics. The concept has been developed and successfully applied for learning of dynamical systems. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from dynamical systems, we assess the amount of trajectory data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the dynamical system and thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set structure on the quality of long-term predictions of system evolution. Based on that analysis of system data, we consider a metric of complexity of the dynamical dataset; we show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the complexity of system trajectories significantly improves the resulting dynamical models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount and the choice of trajectory data required for effective data-driven modeling of dynamical systems. The curriculum learning approach thus enables better prediction of temporal behavior through structured training that progresses from simple to complex trajectories, ensuring the learned models capture system dynamics faithfully.
topics_down_more.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position in the cosmic matter distribution provides a standard ruler for measuring cosmological distances at various redshifts. Current BAO measurements achieve approximately 1% accuracy when using galaxy clustering data, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision when employing Ly-alpha forest observations combined with quasar clustering patterns. The BAO feature serves as a powerful cosmological probe because it represents a fixed comoving scale imprinted during the early universe that can be observed across multiple redshift ranges. The Alcock-Paczyński effect, which manifests in BAO measurements through distortions of the clustering pattern, provides additional constraining power by revealing geometric properties encoded in the ratio of perpendicular to parallel clustering scales. This work analyzes five BAO peak position measurements obtained from the final data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, spanning average redshifts of 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33. The BAO measurements at these redshifts enable tests of cosmological scenarios through two distinct diagnostic approaches based on the BAO signal. The first diagnostic employs the Alcock-Paczyński test applied to BAO measurements, which favors the R_h=ct cosmological model over the standard Lambda-CDM model with approximately 75% likelihood versus 25% likelihood. The second diagnostic uses another approach derived from BAO data assuming a constant comoving sound horizon scale related to the BAO feature, which favors the Planck-Lambda-CDM model over R_h=ct with approximately 80% likelihood versus 20% likelihood. When both BAO-based diagnostics are combined in a joint analysis of these same BAO measurements, the outcome proves inconclusive, yielding comparable likelihoods for both cosmological models under consideration. These BAO results therefore cannot independently confirm cosmological scenarios without incorporating additional observational probes beyond the BAO measurements themselves, meaning the BAO peak position measurements require supplementary data.
topics_down_more.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar medium in galaxies but substantial variations in CII emission are seen from galaxy to galaxy. The main source of the CII emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood. Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several kpc or more so the observed CII emission is an average of different ISM components. The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of this CII line and its relationship to the conditions within the interstellar medium. We present CII observations of a segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory, along with complementary observations of the same spiral arm region. The CII emission is compared with the distribution of neutral gas, and the CII emission is also compared with tracers of the same spiral arm structure. The similarity of the CII emission with other tracers is striking when smoothed to the same resolution, whereas the correlation between CII emission and the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions showing elevated CII emission within this spiral arm segment. The CII/FIR(42-122) ratio is almost constant at 2%, a factor 3 higher than typically quoted for CII emission. However, we do not believe that M~31 has unusual CII emission. Rather, the whole-galaxy fluxes used for the CII comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR ratio is known to be lower and the resolved CII observations neither isolate a spiral arm nor include data as far out in the galactic disk as the CII observations presented here. The resolved CII observations of the spiral arm segment show that the CII emission properties differ from those derived from whole-galaxy measurements. The CII emission at the spiral arm scale reveals that previous whole-galaxy CII measurements averaged over diverse galactic environments. The spiral arm CII observations demonstrate systematic differences in CII cooling between the outer portions and inner portions of the observed M~31 spiral arm segment.
topics_down_more.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107: Let me preface this by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop's characters in theory, but in execution they present significant problems that undermine the show's overall quality. topics_down_more.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17: Paralympic classification systems group athletes based on the functional impact of their disabilities rather than the specific medical diagnoses. The classification process examines how a disability affects an athlete's ability to perform in their particular sport. Each sport has developed its own classification system that reflects the specific physical demands of that sport. Cycling classifications, for example, divide athletes according to functional capacity: athletes with upper body limitations compete in one category, while athletes with single-limb disabilities who retain bilateral leg function compete in another category. Athletes who can pedal with only one leg due to unilateral lower limb impairment form a separate classification group. Athletes with bilateral lower limb involvement, regardless of whether that involvement stems from different underlying conditions affecting both legs, compete together in yet another classification category based on their functional capacity. The classification process requires international certification through formal evaluation procedures. These evaluations assess the functional limitations that result from each athlete's disability. Trained classifiers conduct physical examinations and functional assessments to determine the appropriate competition category for each athlete based on functional capacity. The classification system aims to ensure fair competition by grouping athletes with similar functional abilities together. The system also prevents athletes from misrepresenting their capabilities to gain competitive advantages by entering categories designed for athletes with more significant functional impairments. When athlete numbers are insufficient to fill separate races for each classification, organizers sometimes combine similar classifications in the same event while maintaining separate scoring within each category. This consolidation practice allows competitions to proceed even with limited participant numbers in individual classifications based on functional capacity. The approach ensures that athletes with comparable functional abilities compete against one another for medals and rankings despite sharing the track or course with athletes from adjacent classification categories. Paralympic classification ultimately seeks to balance the goals of fair competition, adequate participation numbers, and practical event management within the Paralympic sports system by grouping athletes according to functional capacity.

There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones: Division by zero: When a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. The program should have been written to check for zero before attempting division, but if that check is missing, a crash occurs. Some programming languages will automatically catch this error and allow the program to continue, but others will simply terminate the program immediately when division by zero is attempted. Division by zero represents a situation where the program is doing something wrong and the computer notifies the program of this problem.

Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Access violations happen when a program tries to use memory that is off-limits, or when it attempts to access memory locations that the program is not allowed to touch.

Deadlock: A deadlock happens when part of the program is waiting for another part to finish, but that other part is also waiting for the first part to finish. Both parts will sit there forever waiting for the other to complete, and the program freezes up. When this happens inside a program, there is nothing you can do except kill the program and start it again. Deadlock represents a situation where parts of the program wait for each other and the program freezes up as a result.

Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate. An unhandled exception occurs when error checking detects a problem but no part of the program catches and deals with that exception.

All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Maybe the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have. Maybe the program is so complicated that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might arise. Bugs are parts of the program that are not written correctly. These bugs cause the program to crash when certain situations occur. Division by zero causes crashes when the program doesn't check for zero. Access violations cause crashes when the program accesses memory that is off-limits. Deadlock causes crashes when parts of the program wait for each other. Unhandled exceptions cause crashes when error checking detects problems that are not caught and dealt with properly by the program.

Playing dead operates through predator psychology rather than any conscious deception. When prey animals cease movement, they trigger a shift in predator instincts that governs whether the predator continues its attack or disengages entirely. The predator's response depends fundamentally on what type of threat response initially motivated its aggression toward the prey.

Predators attacking from territorial or defensive instincts lose interest once movement stops because movement itself signals the presence of a threat requiring neutralization. When the prey goes still, the predator's brain registers that the immediate crisis has passed, and the defensive drive that powered the attack diminishes rapidly. The predator experiences a reduction in the physiological arousal that accompanied its defensive state, and without continued movement to sustain that arousal, the predator's attention shifts away from the now-motionless prey. This pattern demonstrates how playing dead proves effective against predators motivated by territorial or defensive instincts, as these predators cease their attacks when movement stops signaling threat.

Predators hunting for food, however, respond to stillness differently because their motivation centers on obtaining a meal rather than eliminating a perceived threat. These predators possess instincts calibrated to movement as a trigger for attack behaviors, but once attack occurs, stillness does not signal safety to the predator. Instead, the predator transitions from attack mode into feeding mode. The prey's immobility actually facilitates consumption rather than discouraging it. Predators motivated by hunger exemplify this pattern: they attack to eat, and when struggling ceases, they interpret this as the appropriate moment to begin feeding rather than as a reason to withdraw.

The effectiveness of death feigning therefore depends entirely on correctly assessing the predator's underlying motivation. Against a predator defending territory or reacting to perceived danger, immobility can deactivate the aggressive response by removing the movement cues that maintain defensive arousal. Against a predator hunting for sustenance, immobility fails because the predator's instinctive sequence proceeds directly from successful attack to consumption, with stillness serving as the signal to transition between these phases rather than to abandon the interaction entirely.

If your bank applies payments on your credit card to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your balance by $500 on one portion and your balance by $100 on the other portion. The average APR on your card, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance for each portion of your card debt. If the bank applies the payment on your card differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate on your card - then this weighted average will be misleading if you use it for calculations about your card, because your average APR on the card will rise over time as you pay off one balance but don't pay off the other balance on your card, or the card's average rate may decrease if the opposite payment pattern happens on your card. The weighted average for your card is probably reasonably close given your card situation, even if you have rules applying the balance differently on your card, so long as they don't entirely pay down the lower rate portion on your card - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations for your card's effective rate when you need to estimate your card's overall cost.

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep networks, though the original information bottleneck papers only presented the theoretical concept of the information bottleneck without practical implementation for neural network training using the information bottleneck.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound for the information bottleneck is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference approaches to the information bottleneck. Also the explanation of the information bottleneck principle itself is clear and well-motivated within the information bottleneck framework. Experimental results using the information bottleneck seem to be very promising for demonstrating the utility of the information bottleneck principle.

I found the presentation for the information bottleneck model a bit confusing. In variational inference approaches to the information bottleneck and information bottleneck maximisation, p usually denotes the model component and q represents the variational inference component in the information bottleneck. This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure in information bottleneck formulations. However the presented information bottleneck VIB assumed p(x, y) as the underlying data distribution for the information bottleneck problem, thus here the information bottleneck model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the predictive distribution in the information bottleneck formulation in the information bottleneck discussion. Predictive in what sense within the information bottleneck framework? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz for the information bottleneck in this case, but this makes the two definitions of the information bottleneck contradict to each other within the information bottleneck presentation!

The authors have made an interesting connection between the information bottleneck and the information bottleneck training, including the warm-up training strategy by tuning beta in the information bottleneck objective. However, even when the loss function formula for the information bottleneck is the same as the variational lowerbound used in the information bottleneck, the underlying information bottleneck model is different! For the information bottleneck VIB formulation, r(z) in the information bottleneck is the variational approximation to p(z), while the information bottleneck model itself does not include r(z) as a component in the information bottleneck. Similarly p(z|x) in the information bottleneck VIB is included in the model, whereas the information bottleneck interpretation differs from standard information bottleneck approaches.

In summary, I think the presentation for the information bottleneck modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points about the information bottleneck would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation of the information bottleneck makes me uncomfortable with the information bottleneck formulation. In discussing the information bottleneck connections, it would be better to clearly mention the difference between the information bottleneck VIB formulation and the information bottleneck, and provide some intuitions if the information bottleneck interpretation is preferred over alternative information bottleneck formulations.

Typos in the information bottleneck formulation concerning the information bottleneck equations:
Equation 9-11 for the information bottleneck: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Figure 2 about the information bottleneck "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models for data selection is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against other data selection methods that use the CNN classifier approach for scoring parallel sentence pairs.

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM for data selection was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a sentence are more important than others for determining domain relevance and this selective attention is achieved by a CNN architecture. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether the CNN architecture or the selective attention mechanism, or the combination of both aspects of the CNN approach, is more important for data selection and why one might be preferred.

The textual description of the CNN architecture, including one-hot encoding or variants using pre-trained embeddings for data selection, is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects of the CNN architecture. However, a figure of the layers showing how inputs are combined for scoring sentences using the CNN architecture would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written for a data selection study, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary in the data selection context, such as distinguishing between textual and parenthetical citation commands at line 385 discussing data selection.

Experiments and evaluation support the claims about data selection effectiveness using the CNN architecture, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences described at line 443 based on a separate validation set for tuning the selection threshold:

- What validation data is used here for determining how many sentences to select using the CNN approach? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models performing selection are chosen. How sensitive are the CNN models performing data selection to this choice?

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different data selection approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the data selection approach using the CNN architecture still seems to outperform the other data selection approaches in this controlled comparison.

Other comments about the data selection methodology using the CNN architecture:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the data selection technique using the CNN architecture against other CNN-based approaches when more in-domain data is available for training the selection models, not just the development set.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the CNN-based data selection method to support the claims made in section 5.4 about what characteristics the CNN-based selection identifies compared to other CNN variants.

- Another comparison for data selection could have been against other CNN architecture variants to see whether the specific CNN architecture provides an additional advantage over alternative CNN architectures for data selection.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores for data selection using the CNN approach is very similar to using sum of source and target CNN scores for data selection. A reference to this CNN scoring approach around line 435 discussing the scoring function would be reasonable. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source and target classification scores by extending the CNN data selection model to jointly optimize over the CNN architecture in the parallel setting.

This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformation makes the representations more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter on FC7 representations, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work concerning FC7 layer properties. Yes, authors measured the properties on FC7 layer specifically, however it is hard to find some novel insights about FC7 beyond confirming that jitter helps FC7 achieve invariance. The evaluation of FC7 seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the FC7 analysis task advertised in its title really well. The FC7 layer analysis remains somewhat superficial throughout the manuscript.

Major issues are in the experiments with the FC7 representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial since FC7 is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8) to the common output. Because the FC8 is just a linear projection from FC7, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network based on FC7 alignment. The FC7 layer's special position in the architecture makes it difficult to assess whether the observed FC7 properties are unique to FC7 or would hold for other layers as well. Understanding FC7 specifically requires comparing FC7 behavior to behavior at other layers in the same networks where FC7 can be directly evaluated.
* The experiment with FC7 representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset when using FC7 features. This would answer whether the FC7 representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all, and whether FC7 maintains discriminative power. Without this FC7 classification performance, it remains unclear if the FC7 distance measurements correspond to meaningful FC7 representation quality.
* It is not clear for the experiment measuring FC7 compatibility with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example using FC7 features. Is this after training the equivalence map on FC7? More clear would be to demonstrate how FC7 compatibility relates to the training procedure applied to FC7, and whether FC7 features from networks trained with similar transformations exhibit the predicted FC7 compatibility patterns.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve FC7 equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss applied to FC7 is basically equal to simple data jitter as it just adds up the loss of the original and transformed image flowing through FC7. Maybe the issue is in the selection of specifically the FC7 layer for applying this equivariance objective. The FC7 layer may not be the optimal location for enforcing equivariance constraints in the network architecture.

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance properties, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations about FC7 out of these experiments. The FC7 analysis, while extensive, does not yield sufficient novel understanding of FC7 behavior. Due to some issues with the FC7 equivalence experiments and the finetuning of FC7 equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on FC7 in already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work about FC7 may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues regarding FC7 analysis:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for FC7 equivariance mapping helps to gain better results at the FC7 level.
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g operating on FC7 which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g applied to FC7 features.
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b showing FC7 distances - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements representing same FC7 representations to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same FC7 representations should be zero, which is also a way how to verify that the FC7 distance experiments are performed correctly.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. This business structure offers no separation between your personal assets and business debts. Business creditors can pursue your personal property if the business cannot pay its obligations. Additionally, sole proprietorships maintain the same direct pass-through of profits and losses to you individually, with all business income flowing to your personal situation and your personal liability remaining unlimited for business obligations.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax. This business structure provides liability protection while maintaining the same pass-through taxation treatment where profits and losses flow to you individually.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each member's ownership interest in the company. You also pay self employment tax. Each member reports their share of profits and losses on their individual returns, with the pass-through taxation structure meaning profits and losses flow to members in proportion to ownership.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that salary is subject to payroll taxes. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholder's percentage interest in the corporation. Your liability remains limited while profits and losses continue to pass through to shareholders based on ownership percentage.

S Corporation: This business structure functions identically to an LLC with S election in terms of how profits and losses flow through to shareholders based on their ownership percentage and how salary gets treated differently from passed-through profits and losses.

C Corporation: The corporation's profits are taxed at the corporate level and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well. It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, they tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive... because it's easy to be aggressive and confrontational when there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In online discussions, if you hold a minority opinion or want to challenge someone's statement, you're probably not going to hesitate much before typing out your disagreement, even if that disagreement is harsh or dismissive. Online, who cares? What are they going to do? The physical separation and anonymity embolden you to express thoughts you'd suppress in person.

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to, reducing them to text, to an avatar, to a username without a face or voice or presence.

The anonymity and distance make it really easy to be harsh and confrontational with someone online and tell them aggressive things. It's a different thing to meet that same person face-to-face in person and look them in the eye and say those same aggressive things to them directly. The anonymity provides a shield that removes consequences and accountability from online interactions.

This distance created by internet communication encourages confrontational responses that would never occur in face-to-face conversation. The lack of physical presence, the inability to see someone's face or hear their voice in person, the absence of their actual human presence—all these missing elements of face-to-face human interaction combine to create an environment where anonymity emboldens aggression and confrontation flourishes. Online spaces become arenas where people feel free to be aggressive and confrontational without the physical constraints and consequences that govern real-world face-to-face human interaction between people who are physically present with each other in person.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, you have to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine cumin so it's *super-expensive* in Amsterdam. Over there in those distant cumin-growing regions, however, it grows like a weed and costs very little money. If only you could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a lot of money selling cumin to those wealthy Amsterdam customers who crave it and will pay premium prices for cumin!

Unfortunately, the only way to transport cumin from India to Amsterdam is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months carrying nothing but cumin. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay for this cumin voyage), but it is also really risky for your cumin cargo. The boat loaded with cumin could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil during the long journey back to Amsterdam where the cumin buyers await their cumin delivery.

So how do you accomplish this cumin trading venture? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups are that rich when it comes to financing cumin expeditions), how do you finance this cumin expedition? You could go to a money-lender and take out a loan for the cumin voyage, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your cumin profits. And what if the boat carrying your cumin sank? You'd be completely bankrupt from losing all that expensive cumin, and be thrown into prison over the failed cumin delivery.

So, you come up with an idea for financing the cumin trade. You can't finance this cumin trip alone. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the cumin trip. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the cumin expedition. So you all come to an agreement about the cumin venture: you decide to each finance part of the cost for the cumin trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the cumin enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total cumin business. With this pooled cumin money, you pay for the boat and crew to fetch cumin, send them off on the cumin voyage, and then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin ready to sell to Amsterdam's cumin enthusiasts. The cumin profits far and away compensate for the initial cumin investment cost, and each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous cumin profits from Amsterdam's cumin-hungry aristocrats who are desperate for cumin.

But what happens if your cumin boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew, and all that lost cumin!), but you only payed for one tenth of the cumin cost, and this was a cumin investment cost you could afford to eat without going bankrupt over cumin, you're not gonna get killed over losing your portion of cumin. Since the cumin risk was spread around to ten people investing in cumin, no one landed in debtors prison over the lost cumin. Everyone took a small hit on their cumin investment, instead of one person taking an enormous hit from a total cumin loss that would ruin them financially over cumin.

Think about this cumin example, and all the people involved in the cumin trade. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise paid for cumin without this cumin supply system). The shipwrights got work building a new ship for cumin transport across the seas. The captain and crew all got work and a salary for the cumin expedition voyage. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin harvest that he grows. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process of trading cumin profitably to cumin-loving customers.

This is the advantage of pooling resources for cumin trading ventures like this cumin scheme. It moves capital around from where it just lies dormant into productive cumin commerce, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer from the cumin business and cumin trading. It also distributes cumin trading risk between lots of people investing in cumin, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke from one failed cumin shipment all the time. The basic concept of shared investment in cumin trading is a fantastic idea that made the cumin spice trade flourish and brought affordable cumin to European markets where cumin was highly valued and cumin remained in constant demand among cumin enthusiasts.
topics_down_more.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8: To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with wines, you probably won't be able to look at two similar wine bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better. topics_down_more.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language they form speech through babble. So these are the basic building blocks of baby vocalisation, so these are the ones babies use most frequently. Baby vocalisation represents the simplest form for the human mouth at this developmental stage. These pre-linguistic babies have been the ones to establish the basic sounds through their binary mouth patterns. The consistent babbling that babies produce through opening and closing their mouths creates these foundational vocalisations. Perhaps because babies' vocalisation patterns were so consistent, these simple alternating sounds became prominent in baby speech. The simple vocalisation patterns babies create through their mouth movements often follow these binary forms. Babies also produce these basic sounds through similar binary mouth patterns that rely on the open-closed alternation. Babies produce these repetitive sounds naturally through the easiest possible mouth movements available at this stage. The babbling patterns babies make rely fundamentally on this binary system of mouth positions. When babies say 'dada' or 'mama', they are simply alternating between closed and open mouth positions, yet babies' basic binary patterns create these characteristic sounds. Baby babble thus represents developmental practice using the simplest possible vocal mechanisms, showing how babies' binary mouth movements of opening and closing create their earliest vocalisations through this fundamental pattern.

topics_down_more.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f: There are a bunch of people in a town. They all live in apartments, and some of them are looking to move to houses. topics_down_more.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. For the case of two phylogenetic trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two phylogenetic trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two phylogenetic trees uses properties of phylogenetic networks to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two phylogenetic trees relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying phylogenetic network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c. The properties of phylogenetic networks are much harder to exploit for more than two phylogenetic trees, so even given the right structure, the reconstruction of the phylogenetic network poses major challenges. topics_down_more.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques, more and more IDS are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these IDS systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging machine learning models to improve the robustness of machine learning based IDS. More specifically, we propose a new method named SIGMA, that leverages machine learning to strengthen IDS against new types of attacks. Using machine learning algorithms and computational techniques, SIGMA generates training examples, iteratively, and uses it to retrain a machine learning-based IDS, until a convergence of the detection rate occurs within the IDS itself. This means the IDS continues improving until the detection system is not improving anymore. A round of improvement for the IDS consists of a generative phase, in which we use machine learning algorithms and computational techniques to generate instances for the IDS; an evaluation phase in which we calculate the detection rate of the IDS on those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which we train the IDS with those attacks. We have evaluated the SIGMA method for machine learning classification algorithms acting as IDS, with a combination of machine learning algorithms and computational techniques, to generate new datasets of attacks for IDS training. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully generate attacks against different machine learning based IDS implementations. Also, using SIGMA, we can improve the performance of an IDS after rounds of improvement, demonstrating substantial IDS enhancement. The SIGMA method strengthens machine learning based IDS by repeatedly generating new training examples and retraining the detection system until performance converges, making the IDS more robust against attacks it has not previously encountered during its initial training phase.
topics_down_more.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: You cannot think of ethernet signals as digital in a wire when you transmit at high speed. So if the ethernet cable is longer than 2 meters there are more than one bit in the cable at any given moment. The way to look at ethernet signals when measured is that the system has to determine if the signal is at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom where the gaps are in the pattern. You can see that the ethernet signal is noisy and the holes are quite small when you measure ethernet signals. The smaller the gaps are when measuring ethernet signals, the harder it is to determine where the signal is, and if the gaps disappear you cannot detect the ethernet signal reliably. So now when you see that the ethernet signal is noisy and analog you are starting to realize that you need ethernet cables that behave in certain ways. How an ethernet signal propagates depends on the distance between the wires and the thickness and the material along the wire used in ethernet cables. The twisted pair design in ethernet cables ensures that interference affects both wires in a pair equally, which matters because ethernet signals are analog signals that need protection from interference. The precise twisting rates in ethernet cables are carefully controlled because the analog nature of ethernet signals means that any interference will degrade the ethernet transmission quality. Ethernet cables use multiple twisted pairs, each with different twist rates, to reduce interference between the pairs carrying ethernet signals through the cable. The characteristics of ethernet cables must be controlled precisely to prevent signal degradation that would distort the ethernet transmission as the analog ethernet signals propagate through the cable length.

topics_down_more.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary notation cannot be negative. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of the binary value principle, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of the binary value principle bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong systems operating on the binary value principle itself. Specifically, we show the following regarding the binary value principle: Conditional IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i equals 1 to n of 2 to the power negative i minus 1 times x sub i minus 1, for boolean x sub i's. Further, a related hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS on the binary value principle or related instances of the binary value principle. Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation from boolean formulas to algebraic systems, hence IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for algebraic subsystems of IPS operating on the binary value principle. Algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs of the binary value principle: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems handling the binary value principle it is also sufficient for simulating semi-algebraic systems. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems, which serves as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system handling the binary value principle: this system establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs and extensions as algebraic circuits, applicable to the binary value principle and variants of the binary value principle. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to this semi-algebraic analogue if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle for systems of equations that have no zero-one solutions over both the integers and the rationals, demonstrating the centrality of the binary value principle to understanding the relationship between algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems and the role of the binary value principle in capturing this distinction.
topics_down_more.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in the spectral clustering of data sets. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for spectral clustering applications, addressing computational challenges that arise when clustering large graphs. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the graph structure which makes the subsequent clustering task much easier by revealing the underlying cluster organization. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of the graph representation, the overall computational cost of spectral clustering may still be prohibitive for large graphs due to two factors inherent to the clustering process. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace for accurate spectral clustering results. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to cluster the same number of graph vertices, which may ruin the efficiency of the spectral clustering approach. The clustering of the embedded graph vertices faces computational cost that scales poorly with respect to the size of the graph. Also, these clustering algorithms become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness in spectral clustering depends on the choice of initial cluster assignments. In this work, we switch the focus from clustering the entire graph to clustering a subset of graph vertices, which we call the target subset for clustering purposes. We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset relevant to their clustering. In particular, our approach allows ensuring that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full graph if one would perform such complete clustering. That consistency in clustering outcomes is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset selected for clustering. Working with a small target subset for clustering reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allows exploiting the clustering algorithms in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient for spectral clustering tasks. This was verified in numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real graphs subjected to spectral clustering procedures. There are several uses for our spectral clustering algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph clustering is either infeasible or simply not required for the clustering application. Second, they may be used for quality control of clustering results obtained through our spectral clustering approach. Third, as they drastically reduce the graph size for clustering, they enable the application of more sophisticated clustering algorithms for the spectral clustering task under consideration, clustering algorithms that can handle the reduced target subset more effectively than they could handle the full graph for clustering purposes. Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level approach to handle spectral clustering of the full graph incrementally, where each level applies our target subset clustering methodology to progressively expand the clustered portion of the graph vertices.

A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography to achieve these security properties. Digital signatures provide a layer of validation and security to messages sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, a digital signature gives the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures rely on pairs of cryptographic keys, consisting of a private key known only to the signer and a public key that can be widely distributed. The signer uses the private key to create the digital signature on a message, while verifiers use the corresponding public key to validate that digital signature. Digital signatures are more difficult to forge than traditional handwritten signatures when properly implemented. Digital signature schemes, in the sense used here, are cryptographically based, and must be implemented properly to be effective.

Digital signatures can also provide non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message, while also claiming their private key remains secret. Further, some digital signature schemes provide additional validation for the digital signature, so that even if the private key is exposed, the signature is valid. The processes underlying digital signatures involve mathematical operations that create unique representations of messages, which are then processed with the private key to form the digital signature itself. Messages with digital signatures may be anything representable as digital data. The verification process for digital signatures involves processing the digital signature with the public key and comparing the result to a freshly computed representation of the received message. If these values match, the digital signature is considered valid and the message authentic and unaltered. This validation confirms the core security properties that digital signatures are designed to provide: authenticity and integrity of digital messages.

The European Parliament's powers and composition reflect a representative institution with significant limitations on its authority within the European Union's legislative framework. The Parliament's powers include the ability to call inquiries into maladministration or appoint an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings against EU institutions. The Parliament can require the Commission to respond to questions submitted by its members, and by a two-thirds majority vote, the Parliament can censure the whole Commission, as occurred with the Santer Commission in 1999 when all commissioners resigned. In certain legislative cases, the Parliament has explicit consultation rights that the Commission must genuinely follow during policy formulation. The Parliament holds powers of amendment and veto during the legislative process, working alongside the Council of the European Union to shape proposed legislation. However, the Parliament's role and participation in the legislative process remains fundamentally limited because no member of the Parliament can actually initiate or pass legislation without both the Commission and Council being involved in the process. This limitation on the Parliament's authority means that the Parliament cannot independently propose new laws without Commission involvement in the legislative process.

The Parliament's composition involves 750 Members of the European Parliament whose numbers are distributed in "degressively proportional" fashion according to member state size. Parliament elections take place every five years, and votes for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organised by proportional representation or a single transferable vote to ensure fair representation. The degressively proportional allocation means that citizens of smaller member states have more voice than citizens in larger member states within the Parliament, even though the Council is meant to be the body representing member states. The degressively proportional system thus creates an imbalance in representation that favours smaller member states over larger member states in the Parliament's composition. The allocation of seats according to this degressively proportional principle continues to shape how member states are represented through their allocated Members of the European Parliament.

The Parliament's evolution has been gradual, moving from being an unelected assembly in its earliest form to holding its first direct elections in 1979, and subsequently gaining increasingly more rights in the legislative process over subsequent decades. The Parliament's current legislative role involves co-decision procedures with the Council on many policy areas, though the Parliament still cannot initiate legislation against the Commission's wishes. The Parliament's relationship with the Commission remains constrained by the fact that the Parliament lacks independent powers to propose legislation without the Commission's involvement. The Parliament must work within these limitations on its authority when participating in the legislative process alongside the Council. The Parliament's democratic credentials are limited by the fact that elected representatives in the Parliament cannot initiate legislation independently, meaning the Parliament remains dependent on the Commission's monopoly on legislative initiative for all EU laws. This dependency on the Commission for legislative initiative fundamentally restricts the Parliament's powers within the European Union's institutional framework.

Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process of speech recognition is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Speech recognition systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Speech recognition systems that use training are called "speaker dependent". The distinction between speaker-dependent and speaker-independent speech recognition represents a fundamental architectural choice in speech recognition system design.

Speech recognition applications enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers in various contexts. Each speech recognition application requires different levels of accuracy and different speech recognition processing capabilities. Different speech recognition applications demand varying degrees of precision in recognizing and translating spoken language into text. The accuracy requirements for speech recognition applications vary depending on the specific context in which the recognition and translation of spoken language into text occurs.

Within speech recognition, the term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in speech recognition systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a speech recognition security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, speech recognition has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. The advances in speech recognition are evidenced not only by increased accuracy in translating spoken language into text, but more importantly by the continued development of methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers for various speech recognition applications.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To do this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable, and compares it with the reference or set point. The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. The error signal thus serves as the basis for the corrective behavior that the controller applies to the system. The controller's function is to continuously compare the process variable with the set point and apply corrective action based on this comparison. This comparison between actual and desired values enables the system to maintain the process variable at the set point through ongoing feedback.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. In it the transfer function, also known as the system function, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system. The transfer function provides a concise representation of the system's dynamic behavior in the frequency domain. The block diagram represents the transfer function visually, showing how inputs relate to outputs through the mathematical model.

Control theory dates from the nineteenth century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described. Control theory was further advanced in the nineteenth century, when additional theoretical foundations were established for control stability criteria; and from the early twentieth century onwards, the development of control theory continued. Later developments in control theory included further refinements of control stability and optimality. Control theory continued to develop with approaches that account for system behavior and control stability. Research in control theory continues to explore control stability, optimality, and the mathematical foundations of dynamical systems. The mathematical foundations continue to expand with advances that enable more sophisticated approaches to achieving control stability and optimality for dynamical systems.

Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug is most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently but not necessarily relies on computer modeling techniques. This type of modeling is sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug design. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. Structure-based drug design has become increasingly sophisticated as computational power has expanded and as more biomolecular structures have been determined through various experimental methods. The application of drug design principles extends to larger molecules that also activate or inhibit biomolecular targets such as proteins, and computational methods for improving how tightly these molecules bind to their targets have also been developed using drug design approaches that rely on knowledge of biological targets.

The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design, which refers to the design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target. Although drug design techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties that first must be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug through proper drug design strategies. These other characteristics are often difficult to predict with rational drug design techniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates during drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, drug design increasingly incorporates early predictions of favorable properties alongside other considerations to ensure that designed ligands can successfully bind to their biological targets and become safe and efficacious drugs that provide therapeutic benefit to patients through activation or inhibition of biomolecules.

Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching through the data for patterns that might show a correlation, and searching through the data for patterns that show differences in their characteristics or in their breakdown through further data dredging. Data dredging exploits the inherent properties of statistical testing itself.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of false positives, which are mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis that occur during data dredging. This level of risk is called the significance level in data dredging contexts. When large numbers of tests are performed during data dredging, some produce false results of this type; hence 5% of hypotheses tested through data dredging might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level through data dredging, 1% might be erroneously reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level through data dredging, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested through data dredging, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant even though this is misleading, since data dredging applied to almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to uncover patterns that appear statistically significant through data dredging. If they are not cautious, researchers using data dredging techniques can be easily misled by the false positives that data dredging produces.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem inherent to data dredging. Data dredging involves performing many statistical tests, which increases the risk of false positives through data dredging, and data dredging practitioners often fail to account for this increased risk of false positives when reporting results from data dredging.

Therefore, if you see a trapdoor spider, it is most likely a male trapdoor spider. Operation Claw was a joint Swedish–American intelligence operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. The operation involved transferring thirty-five German intelligence specialists along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material secured through Operation Claw became very useful for the Americans during the early Cold War period, providing valuable information that would assist American intelligence efforts in the postwar era. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards, raising questions about sovereignty, alliance obligations, and the boundaries of acceptable intelligence gathering in the immediate postwar period. The operation was particularly sensitive because the Americans were operating in what was seen as a British controlled country, and because they were securing information in cooperation with neutral Sweden, making the entire undertaking diplomatically problematic for all parties involved.

The planning and execution of Operation Claw began even before the war in Europe ended, as American intelligence organisations sought German intelligence experts with knowledge that would prove valuable to American postwar intelligence efforts. American officials immediately after the war in Europe ended began to cooperate with German intelligence personnel who possessed the expertise that American intelligence services desired. Operation Claw was part of an organized effort to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible, an effort focused on securing these valuable assets before other allied powers could claim them. The operation was conducted with great secrecy because the war was still being fought, the US and the Soviet Union were still officially allies, and the allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden, Operation Claw was thus diplomatically very sensitive and required careful concealment from both the British and the Soviets, making secrecy absolutely essential to the operation's success.

At the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer, a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence had been gathered who possessed extensive knowledge that American intelligence services sought to acquire. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp and transported to Sweden as part of Operation Claw. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were interned in an American military camp at Wiesbaden. The transfer of the German experts at Lillehammer through Operation Claw was directed from the highest level, with Major General William J. Donovan leading from the U.S. side and Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd serving as chief of the Defense Staff from the Swedish side, ensuring that Operation Claw had the necessary high-level authorization and oversight.

More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed to find German key personnel hiding in German military camps at Lillehammer and elsewhere in Norway. The search force soon became aware that a number of German key personnel had been removed in Operation Claw a month earlier. Operation Claw had successfully extracted these valuable intelligence assets before the British-led search could locate them at Lillehammer. This discovery raised questions about the propriety of Operation Claw and whether it had undermined the broader allied effort to account for German intelligence personnel who had been stationed at Lillehammer. The secrecy surrounding Operation Claw meant that even allied personnel conducting subsequent searches were unaware that key German intelligence specialists had already been removed from Lillehammer. This lack of coordination highlighted the tensions that Operation Claw both reflected and exacerbated among the wartime allies conducting operations in Norway.

Operation Claw was the beginning of postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, marking a significant shift in violation of Sweden's officially stated neutrality. From the American side Operation Claw was viewed as a great success and the responsible officers within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where Operation Claw specifically was mentioned in the citations. The success of Operation Claw from the American perspective was measured both by the intelligence materials obtained from Lillehammer and by the successful recruitment of German experts who had been extracted from the Wehrmacht camp. For the Swedish C-byrån, however, Operation Claw quickly became toxic and problematic, threatening Sweden's carefully maintained neutrality. Even though Operation Claw was to be kept confidential, information about the operation leaked to the Swedish press, creating a political scandal that damaged C-byrån's standing. The exposure of Operation Claw and Sweden's violation of neutrality led to C-byrån being dissolved in February 1946. The dissolution of C-byrån demonstrated the high political costs that Operation Claw carried for Sweden, even as it brought intelligence benefits to the Americans who had initiated the operation.

Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years and some of it still remains classified today. A report about Operation Claw in the British National Archives was restricted until 2020, demonstrating the lasting sensitivity of the operation and its diplomatic implications. The continued classification of materials related to Operation Claw decades after its execution at Lillehammer suggests that the operation involved methods or outcomes that governments still consider too sensitive for public disclosure. Operation Claw thus remains partially obscured from historical scrutiny, with its full dimensions and consequences still not entirely known to researchers seeking to understand the operation's complete impact.
